sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Destination-Based Principle**: VAT is charged where consumption takes place, transferring revenue to the consuming state rather than the producing state.
• **Input Tax Credit (ITC)**: The bedrock mechanism allowing manufacturers and traders to claim a refund or adjustment for tax already paid on raw materials and intermediate goods.
• **Elimination of Cascading Effect**: Unlike traditional single-point or cumulative sales taxes ('tax on tax'), VAT ensures taxation occurs only on the incremental value added at each stage.
• **State-Level Implementation**: Introduced in India on April 1, 2005 (Haryana being the first), replacing the archaic state sales tax regimes under the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers.

items.definition: The credit available to a registered dealer for the tax paid on purchases of inputs used in the course of business against the tax payable on output supplies.

items.term: Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers
items.definition: A landmark institutional body chaired successively by state finance ministers that designed and monitored the rollout of State VAT across India, serving as the precursor to the GST Council.
The phenomenon where tax is levied on a price that already includes tax from a previous production stage, artificially inflating the final retail price.
Origin-based tax levied by the Central government but collected by origin states on inter-state trade, phased out alongside the introduction of VAT and later GST.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Early Adopters**: Haryana (April 1, 2005), followed rapidly by most non-special category states.
• **Laggards & Holdouts**: Uttar Pradesh and few others implemented it later due to political consensus delays.
• **Exclusions**: Petroleum products, crude oil, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel (ATF), and potable alcohol remained under state VAT even after GST implementation.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Lack of uniform tax rates across states (different slabs like 1%, 4%, 12.5%), interstate border check-posts causing logistical delays, and cascading due to non-creditable local levies.
• **Policy Interventions**: Ultimate replacement of State VAT (except on specified items) by the uniform nationwide Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.

items.title: Mnemonic for Non-GST/Retained VAT Items
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "PEAK Petroleum"
• **Decoded Meaning**: P - Petrol/Petroleum crude, E - Electricity (remained under electricity duty), A - Alcohol for human consumption, K - Kerosene/Natural Gas/ATF.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly identifies items kept outside the unified GST framework and retained under old VAT/Excise regimes.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Value Added = Output Value minus Intermediate Consumption. Tax Liability = (Tax Rate × Value Added) equals Output Tax minus Input Tax Credit.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently poses questions implying VAT is a Central tax. Remember that State VAT was legislated and collected exclusively by individual State governments under Entry 54 of the State List (List II) of the Seventh Schedule, prior to Constitutional amendments.

Mains Value Addition: Emphasize how State VAT acted as a vital stepping stone toward cooperative federalism by forcing states to deliberate on uniform floor rates via the Empowered Committee, laying the institutional blueprint for the modern GST Council.

keyTakeaways: VAT eliminated the historical cascading tax burden through the robust Input Tax Credit mechanism.
State-level implementation suffered from inter-state rate wars and lack of uniformity, necessitating the transition to GST.
Certain goods like alcohol and petroleum products continue to be governed by legacy VAT frameworks.
